explanations.explanation: Mercy it is. David says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail…" (Psalm 6:2). He doesn't come in with a list of his good points. He just says he's frail and asks for mercy, and I think that's about the most honest way to walk into any prayer.

Wisdom is a good thing to ask for, but it isn't what David asks for here. He says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail…" (Psalm 6:2). What he asks for is mercy, and it's the very next thing out of his mouth.

Victory sounds like a very kingly thing to ask for, friend. But David doesn't ask for it here. He says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail…" (Psalm 6:2). He asks for mercy, because he knows he's frail.

Not quite, friend. David says the opposite: "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony." (Psalm 6:2). Frail and in agony is not how a man talks when he thinks he can handle it alone. I think that's what makes the prayer so honest.

False is right. David says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony." (Psalm 6:2). He calls himself frail and asks the LORD to heal him. Nobody flexing their muscles prays like that, and I love it.

True it is. In verse 2 his bones are in agony, and then David says, "My soul is deeply distressed." (Psalm 6:3). So it's not only his bones that hurt. Then he asks, "How long, O LORD, how long?" (Psalm 6:3).

Not this time, friend. Verse 2 has his bones in agony, but then David adds, "My soul is deeply distressed." (Psalm 6:3). So it isn't only his bones. His soul is hurting too, and he brings it right to the LORD.

The LORD's loving devotion is right. David says, "Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion." (Psalm 6:4). He doesn't hand the LORD a list of his own good points. He points to the LORD's loving devotion, and I think that's a solid place to stand.

Power isn't the reason David gives, friend. He says, "Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion." (Psalm 6:4). The reason on his lips is the LORD's loving devotion. That's the one to remember.

Reputation is a creative guess, but David doesn't say it. He says, "Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion." (Psalm 6:4). His reason is the LORD's loving devotion, and he doesn't mention anything else.

Not quite, friend. David says, "For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?" (Psalm 6:5). Sheol is the realm of the dead. He says there's no mention of the LORD in death, so he isn't describing the dead praising Him.

False is right. David says, "For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?" (Psalm 6:5). Sheol is the realm of the dead. He says there's no mention of the LORD in death, and then he asks who can praise Him from there.

True. David says, "I am weary from groaning; all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears." (Psalm 6:6). All night, a flooded bed and a drenched couch. I think this one hurts, friend.

Not quite, friend. David says, "I am weary from groaning; all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears." (Psalm 6:6). The weeping goes on all night. I think this part of the psalm hurts.

They fail from grief is right. David says, "My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes." (Psalm 6:7). After a night of weeping, his eyes are giving out. Grief and foes together will do that.

Shining with hope sounds nice, friend, but it isn't what David says. He says, "My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes." (Psalm 6:7). His eyes fail from grief. Hope doesn't show up in this verse.

Seeing more clearly is the opposite of what David says. He says, "My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes." (Psalm 6:7). His eyes grow dim. That's what a night of weeping leaves behind.

explanations.answer: The LORD has heard his weeping
explanations.explanation: The LORD has heard his weeping is right. David says, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping." (Psalm 6:8). That's the "for" in the verse, the reason he gives. A moment ago he was groaning, and now he's telling them to go.

explanations.answer: His tears have finally dried up
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say his tears dried up, friend. He says, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping." (Psalm 6:8). What changed is that the LORD has heard his weeping. That's the reason David gives.

explanations.answer: His army has just shown up
explanations.explanation: No army in this psalm, friend. David says, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping." (Psalm 6:8). The reason he gives isn't a crowd of soldiers. It's that the LORD has heard his weeping.

Accepted is right. David says, "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer." (Psalm 6:9). Verse 8 had the LORD hearing his weeping, and now it's his prayer being accepted. After all that groaning, that's a big turn.
Rejected is the opposite of what David says. He says, "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer." (Psalm 6:9). The word is accepts. His prayer isn't turned away.

Delayed is a fair guess after "How long, O LORD, how long?" (Psalm 6:3). But in verse 9 David says, "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer." The word he uses is accepts. He doesn't say delayed anywhere.

explanations.answer: They will turn back in disgrace
explanations.explanation: They will turn back in disgrace is right. David says, "All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace." (Psalm 6:10). Notice the word sudden. The psalm that started with groaning ends with enemies turning back.

explanations.answer: They will win in the end
explanations.explanation: Winning in the end is not what David says, friend. He says, "All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace." (Psalm 6:10). It's his enemies who will be ashamed and dismayed, and they turn back.

Becoming his friends is a kind thought, but David doesn't say it. He says, "All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace." (Psalm 6:10). They will be ashamed and dismayed, and they turn back. Friendship doesn't show up in this verse.
